analysis.investment_thesis: CSB Bank trades marginally below its Graham Number (₹399.9 vs. calculated ₹457) with a P/E of 11.16 and P/B of 1.48, meeting several quantitative thresholds — yet finance costs are compounding at 33.8% CAGR against revenue growth of only 20.5%, squeezing the spread and decelerating net profit growth to a mere 4.8% in the latest year. The margin of safety is too thin and the earnings trajectory too weak to justify a confident purchase.
key_strengths: Trades below Graham Number (₹399.9 vs. ₹457 calculated), the most fundamental valuation test I apply
P/E of 11.16 (well under my 15x ceiling) and forward P/E of 7.86 suggest the market prices in limited optimism
Four consecutive years of positive net profit (₹458 → ₹547 → ₹567 → ₹594 Cr) satisfies my minimum earnings continuity requirement
key_risks: Finance costs compounding at 33.8% CAGR (₹885 → ₹2,121 Cr) — rising far faster than revenue (20.5%) — signals severe NIM compression and deteriorating lending economics
Net profit growth has nearly stalled: only 4.8% YoY in FY2025 (₹567→₹594 Cr) despite 18.8% revenue growth, implying the spread squeeze is worsening

Operating cash flow was deeply negative in FY2025 (−₹5,256 Cr), reflecting aggressive loan book expansion funded largely by a tripling of debt (₹1,757→₹5,246 Cr) — leverage rising at an uncomfortable pace
red_flags: Finance cost CAGR (33.8%) more than 1.6× revenue CAGR (20.5%) — a bank's core economics are deteriorating, not improving
OCF positive in only 2 of 4 years; FY2025 FCF of −₹5,556 Cr is not merely loan-book growth noise at this scale
P/B of 1.48 sits precisely at my upper boundary — there is virtually no book-value cushion if asset quality deteriorates
analysis.detailed_analysis:
CSB Bank passes several of my arithmetic filters that most stocks fail: the price of ₹399.9 falls below the Graham Number of approximately ₹457 (derived from EPS ≈ ₹35 and BVPS ≈ ₹266), the P/E of 11.16 is comfortably under 15, and the P/B of 1.48 is just inside my 1.5 ceiling. The bank has an unbroken four-year profit record and 40% promoter ownership by Fairfax India (a disciplined capital allocator), which provides some governance comfort. Revenue has grown at a healthy 20.5% CAGR, and total equity has risen from ₹2,651 Cr to ₹4,498 Cr, strengthening the book.

However, the numbers that trouble me most are the ones inside the income statement. Finance costs have grown at 33.8% CAGR — outpacing revenue growth by more than 13 percentage points — which means the bank is paying depositors and lenders progressively more while earning proportionally less on loans. The consequence is plain: net profit growth has slowed from 19.5% in FY2023 to a mere 4.8% in FY2025. For a bank, earning power *is* intrinsic value, and earning power here is eroding. I also note that operating cash flow swung to −₹5,256 Cr in FY2025 and borrowings nearly tripled in a single year. Rapid loan-book expansion can mask credit problems that only surface in the next credit cycle. At a P/B of 1.48 with no meaningful safety buffer against book erosion, I cannot call this a bargain — only a modestly priced bank with deteriorating spread dynamics.
